title: Early Screening of Fake Social Media Accounts Under Limited Profile Signals and Time Shift
content: Social media sites often have to decide whether an account is real or fake before it has had a chance to make many posts or build up a history of what it has done. In this study, we examined the efficacy of early identification based solely on brief biographical and fundamental profile information. We used 4,465 tagged accounts from the Cresci-2017 dataset to test this. 3,474 of these were human individuals, and 991 were known bots. We could only examine profile information, simple follower/following numbers, and bio text for the real accounts because we could not see their actual tweet history. Next, we examined three separate "early windows" of account data and compared how effectively Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost could discern the difference between actual and phony accounts. First, we could not segregate the data by date alone because there were no bots in the later time period. To remedy this, we split the timeline into two parts: one for legitimate accounts and another for false accounts. This retained the order of events in each group and helped us determine how well the models held up over time. The second window included the most powerful settings for the model. It added the number of followers, friends, favorites, lists, and follower-to-friend ratio. Extreme Gradient Boosting achieved a precision of 0.9778, a recall of 0.8844, a harmonic mean of precision and recall of 0.9288, and an area under the precision-recall curve of 0.9593 with that setting. Incorporating short descriptive features yielded no measurable performance gains once the core relational indicators were included. Both the feature attribution analysis and the three-way workflow revealed the same finding: a small relational block contained the majority of the valuable early signals. Only 2.35 percent of accounts fell within the review band.
